The relationship involving acid-base imbalance, mineral metabolism and bone health status has previously been reported but the efficacy of the alkalizing supplementation in targeting acid overload and preventing bone loss has not yet been fully elucidated. In this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study, the hypothesis that potassium citrate (K citrate) modifies bone turnover in women with postmenopausal osteopenia was tested. Three hundred and ten women were screened; 40 women met the inclusion criteria and were randomly assigned to the treatment or the placebo group. They were treated with K citrate (30 mEq day −1 ) or a placebo in addition to calcium carbonate (500 mg day −1 ) and vitamin D (400 IU day −1 ). At baseline and time points of 3 and 6 months, serum indicators of renal function, electrolytes, calciotropic hormones, serum bone turnover markers (BTMs) (tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase 5b (TRACP5b), carboxy-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen (CTX), bone alkaline phosphatase (BAP), procollagen type 1 N terminal propeptide (PINP)), and urine pH, electrolytes, and citrate were measured. The follow-up was completed by 17/20 patients in the “K citrate” group and 18/20 patients in the “placebo” group. At baseline, 90% of the patients exhibited low potassium excretion in 24 h urine samples, and 85% of cases had at least one urine parameter associated with low-grade acidosis (low pH, low citrate excretion). After treatment, CTX and BAP decreased significantly in both groups, but subjects with evidence of low-grade acidosis gained significant benefits from the treatment compared to the placebo. In patients with low 24h-citrate excretion at baseline, a 30% mean decrease in BAP and CTX was observed at 6 months. A significant reduction was also evident when low citrate (BAP: −25%; CTX: −35%) and a low pH (BAP: −25%; CTX: −30%) were found in fasting-morning urine. In conclusion, our results suggested that K citrate supplementation improved the beneficial effects of calcium and vitamin D in osteopenic women with a documented potassium and citrate deficit, and a metabolic profile consistent with low-grade acidosis. osteopenia potassium citrate acid-base urolithiasis bone remodeling bone turnover markers 1. Introduction Bone mass tends to peak around the third decade of life, after which a continuous decline of 0.7% per year is considered to be physiologic. After menopause, however, bone loss is accelerated and, on average, women lose approximately 5% of trabecular bone and 1.5% of the total bone mass per year [ 1 ]. Postmenopausal estrogen deficiency is considered to be the major cause of accelerated bone loss [ 2 ]. It is associated with an increased rate of bone turnover, with an elevated number of active bone remodeling units (BRUs) in which the removal of bone by osteoclasts (OCs) prevails over the formation of bone matrix by osteoblasts (OBs) [ 3 , 4 ]. The imbalance between osteogenesis and bone resorption leads first to osteopenia and, subsequently, to osteoporosis, both characterized by decreased bone mineral density (BMD) (T-scores of <−1 and <−2.5, respectively), deterioration of bone microarchitecture, impairment of bone strength and, ultimately, increased susceptibility to fracture [ 5 ]. According to the “International Osteoporosis Foundation”, it is estimated that osteoporosis affects 200 million women worldwide, and the lifetime risk of experiencing fragility fractures to the distal wrist, vertebral body or proximal femur is approximately 30–35% for women over 50 years of age [ 6 ]. Disability due to osteoporotic fractures notably compromises the activities of daily living (ADL). Actually, the level of self-sufficiency is significantly decreased in 50% of women with hip fractures, and approximately 20% are candidates for long-term institutionalization [ 6 ]. Moreover, the risk of mortality in patients with fractures of the proximal femur is at least double with respect to an age-matched population [ 7 ]. While the highest rate of fractures is found in osteoporotic women, the absolute number is higher in osteopenic women due to the number of subjects with this condition [ 8 ]. This suggests that the risk profile of osteopenic women should be carefully evaluated shortly after menopause in order to identify the multiple factors which may promote bone frailty and make a “fracture event” more likely [ 8 , 9 ]. The risk of fracture is commonly evaluated by algorithms, i.e., the FRAX ® tool ( https://www.sheffield.ac.uk/FRAX/ ) [ 10 ]. However, the evaluation of additional risk factors could be useful for identifying osteopenic women who may benefit from specific measures aimed at preventing bone loss. Among the risk factors, it is well recognized that the proper intake of calcium and vitamin D plays an important role in preserving bone mass, but there are also other factors which seem to influence BMD [ 2 ]. For instance, adverse metabolic conditions (e.g., a high acid load) may increase the rate of bone loss and favor the onset and progression of osteopenia [ 11 ]. In fact, the skeleton is an alkaline reservoir which plays a pivotal role in maintaining the acid-base balance since it is able to modify the composition of the bone mineral matrix by acting as an “ion exchange column” and recovering alkali groups from hydroxyapatite in order to neutralize the proton excess [ 12 ]. In addition, it has been proven that acidosis directly influences the OC and OB activity. In fact, while OCs are virtually inactive at a pH of 7.4, the resorbing properties are stimulated when the pH drops below 6.9. The acidic milieu also significantly inhibits the osteogenic function, including the production of extracellular matrix, the activity of alkaline phosphatase, and the formation of trabecular bone [ 12 ]. A chronic subclinical inflammatory status [ 13 ], diets rich in salt and meat protein [ 14 ] as well as decreased renal function due to aging [ 15 ] are some of the conditions which determine low-grade acidosis. This is a metabolic condition in which the high acid load may exceed the physiological neutralization capacity while maintaining the blood pH within the normal range (7.35–7.45), albeit at values close to the lower limit [ 14 ]. While the nutritional hypothesis has been amended in systematic reviews and meta-analyses [ 11 , 16 , 17 ], the relationship between renal function, and the risk of osteoporosis or hip fracture has been confirmed in many studies. Recent findings have demonstrated that increased acid excretion [ 18 ], dysregulation of calcium homeostasis [ 19 ] and a decrease in urinary citrate [ 20 , 21 , 22 ] are recognizable in patients who exhibit osteopenia/osteoporosis and high bone turnover, thus, suggesting that urinary metabolic profiling may have significant implications for monitoring bone health status. Since low pH is a risk factor which accelerates bone loss, some authors have proposed using strategies capable of opposing the acid overload as measures for preventing osteopenia progression or for supporting the treatment of osteoporosis. Proton pump inhibitors could be an effective strategy since these drugs have been designed specifically for counteracting proton excess [ 23 ]. However, they are not recommended for long-term treatment as they seem to enhance fracture risk by inhibiting calcium absorption [ 24 ]. Alternatively, alkalizing supplements have been proposed as a valid tool for limiting the adverse effects of acidosis and delaying bone loss [ 25 ]. For instance, potassium citrate (K citrate) is an alkaline compound used to increase urinary pH and prevent the precipitation of solutes in the urinary tract [ 26 ]. Previous in vitro studies demonstrated that K citrate is capable of preventing the adverse biological effects which a low extracellular pH induces on human bone cells [ 27 ]. A recent meta-analysis has shown that the daily administration of alkalizing supplements, including K citrate, for a time span ranging from 6 months to 2 years, led to a significant reduction in acid and calcium excretion, and a reduction in bone resorption, thus, suggesting a potential benefit to bone health [ 25 ]. However, the authors highlighted the significant heterogeneity of the studies, as the dosages, duration of treatment, patient inclusion criteria, primary outcomes and endpoints were very different. As a consequence, valid evidence in support of beginning the use of K citrate supplementation is still lacking. To test the hypothesis that the daily administration of K citrate would be able to modify serum markers of bone resorption and formation, we performed a six-month prospective study in a homogeneous cohort of women with postmenopausal osteopenia. Moreover, laboratory parameters which could be useful in recognizing the osteopenic women who may benefit from the alkalizing treatment were searched for.

extracted_data.document_summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot study investigated the effects of 6-month potassium citrate (K citrate) supplementation (30 mEq/day), in combination with calcium and vitamin D, on bone turnover markers and urinary metabolic profiles in 40 postmenopausal women with osteopenia. The study found that while bone turnover markers (CTX and BAP) decreased in both K citrate and placebo groups, K citrate significantly enhanced these beneficial effects, particularly in a subgroup of patients with pre-existing low-grade acidosis (low urine pH and/or low potassium and citrate excretion). K citrate also improved urinary pH, citrate, and potassium excretion. The study concluded that K citrate is beneficial for osteopenic women with documented potassium/citrate deficits and low-grade acidosis, but its indiscriminate use is not recommended without such evidence.

treatment_details.dose_specificity: Daily oral supplementation with 30 mEq of K citrate (in two tablets) for 6 months. This was administered in addition to daily calcium carbonate (500 mg day   ⁻¹) and vitamin D (400 IU day   ⁻¹) for all subjects (K citrate and placebo groups). The K citrate treatment showed significant benefits in subjects with evidence of low-grade acidosis (low 24h-citrate excretion or low fasting-morning urine pH) compared to the placebo, with significant changes observed as early as 3 months. No specific dose-response comparisons were reported, and adherence rates were approximately 90% for both groups.

analyzed_biomarkers.biomarker_name: Carboxy-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen (CTX)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Decreased significantly in both K citrate and placebo groups. In patients with low 24h-citrate excretion at baseline, a 30% mean decrease was observed at 6 months. A 35% reduction was evident in patients with low fasting-morning urine citrate, and a 30% reduction in patients with low fasting-morning urine pH. Changes induced by K citrate were more evident from three to six months and statistically significant in subgroups with low baseline pH and low citrate excretion. These changes were similar to those observed after antiresorptive drugs, with a reduction greater than 30% correlating with a significant decrease in osteoporotic fracture incidence.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Marker of bone resorption, indicating the breakdown of type I collagen, a major structural component of bone matrix, and reflecting osteoclast activity.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: K citrate (30 mEq day   ⁻¹) supplementation for 6 months, combined with calcium carbonate (500 mg day   ⁻¹) and vitamin D (400 IU day   ⁻¹), in postmenopausal women with osteopenia, particularly those with low 24h-citrate excretion or low fasting-morning urine pH at baseline, and those receiving calcium and vitamin D treatment.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: A decrease indicates reduced bone resorption, suggesting improved bone health and potential reduction in osteoporosis progression. Considered a useful tool for assessing response to anti-osteoporotic drugs and recommended by international committees as a reference marker for bone resorption. Reflects bone remodeling unit (BRU) activity and correlates with bone loss.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Decreased significantly in both K citrate and placebo groups. In patients with low 24h-citrate excretion at baseline, a 30% mean decrease was observed at 6 months. A 25% reduction was evident in patients with low fasting-morning urine citrate, and a 25% reduction in patients with low fasting-morning urine pH. Changes in BAP in the last three-month period were significantly different only in subjects with a low pH in fasting-morning urine. More pronounced decrease after K citrate supplementation was observed in subjects with low urine pH and/or low citrate excretion, compared to calcium and vitamin D alone. These changes were similar to those observed after antiresorptive drugs.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Marker of bone formation, reflecting the activity of osteoblasts (bone-forming cells) and bone matrix maturation. It is an isoenzyme of alkaline phosphatase specific to osteoblasts.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: K citrate (30 mEq day   ⁻¹) supplementation for 6 months, combined with calcium carbonate (500 mg day   ⁻¹) and vitamin D (400 IU day   ⁻¹), in postmenopausal women with osteopenia, particularly those with low 24h-citrate excretion or low fasting-morning urine pH at baseline, and those receiving calcium and vitamin D treatment.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: A decrease indicates reduced bone formation. In the context of accelerated bone loss with increased turnover, a reduction in both resorption and formation markers suggests a rebalancing of bone remodeling towards a healthier state and a beneficial effect on bone health. Reflects bone remodeling unit (BRU) activity and correlates with bone loss. Considered a useful tool for assessing response to anti-osteoporotic drugs, with decreased levels indicating opposition to bone loss progression.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly more elevated in the K citrate group in both fasting-morning and 24 h urine. An increase was found in both patient groups, but the effect over time was significant only after K citrate supplementation. At baseline, 85% of cases had at least one urine parameter associated with low-grade acidosis, including low pH. Low pH (<5.5) was found in 22.5% of 24h urine and 35% of fasting-morning urine samples. Low urine pH was found in a smaller group, especially in fasting-morning urine, correlating with lower potassium and citrate excretion. K citrate is an alkaline compound used to increase urinary pH.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicates the acidity or alkalinity of urine, reflecting systemic acid-base balance, which influences mineral solubility, osteoclast/osteoblast activity, and the solubility of urinary salts, impacting kidney stone formation.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Postmenopausal osteopenia, low-grade acidosis (characterized by low urine pH), K citrate supplementation (30 mEq day   ⁻¹ for 6 months) aimed at counteracting acid overload, particularly in those with baseline low urinary pH.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Low urine pH is associated with low-grade acidosis, which accelerates bone loss and inhibits osteogenic function. Increasing urine pH is a strategy to prevent osteopenia progression and improve bone health. Indicator of renal acid-base regulation and risk of kidney stone formation. Low urine pH is a sign of low-grade acidosis.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly more elevated in the K citrate group in both fasting-morning and 24 h urine. At baseline, low total citrate excretion (≤3.3 mmol day   ⁻¹) was observed in 57.5% of 24h cases, and a low citrate/creatinine ratio (≤0.3 mmol mol   ⁻¹) in 32.5% of 24h cases. In fasting-morning urine, low citrate concentration (≤3.3 mmol L   ⁻¹) was found in 62.5% of cases, and a low citrate/creatinine ratio in 25%. Significant changes were observed as early as 3 months. Highly significant correlation with potassium excretion (R=0.47, p=0.002). Below the threshold value in a considerable proportion of subjects. Lower citrate excretion was observed in postmenopausal women and subjects with low bone mass. Treatment benefits, including 30% mean decreases in BAP and CTX for patients with low 24h-citrate excretion, and 25-35% reductions in BAP and CTX for patients with low fasting-morning urine citrate, were observed.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Chelates calcium, inhibits stone formation, and plays a role in acid-base balance. Its excretion levels can indicate metabolic acidosis/alkalosis. Citrate is necessary for the stability of hydroxyapatite nanocrystal/collagen complexes. Estrogen deficiency and aging are involved in lowering citrate excretion.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Postmenopausal osteopenia, low-grade acidosis (associated with decreased urinary citrate), K citrate supplementation (30 mEq day   ⁻¹ for 6 months) to address citrate deficit and acid overload, particularly in those with baseline low urinary citrate excretion. K citrate supplementation provides citrate.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Decreased urinary citrate is recognized in patients with osteopenia/osteoporosis and high bone turnover, suggesting it as a risk factor for bone loss. Correcting this deficit is associated with reduced bone turnover markers, indicating improved bone health. Increased urinary citrate levels are associated with reduced risk of kidney stone formation and improved mineral metabolism. Low citrate excretion is a defect that significantly benefits from K citrate supplementation. Diminished citrate excretion in postmenopausal women indicates a 'net citrate loss' due to estrogen deficiency, which can accompany disruption of bone microarchitecture. Normalized indicator of renal acid load and protective factor against kidney stone formation; directly influenced by K citrate supplementation.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly higher in the K citrate group compared to the placebo group. At baseline, potassium excretion was <50 mEq in 90% of samples. Significant differences observed as early as 3 months. Below the threshold value in a considerable proportion of subjects. Low potassium excretion was the most frequent urine alteration, with lower excretion correlating with lower citrate excretion and urine pH.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Maintenance of electrolyte balance, kidney function, and regulation of urinary pH and citrate excretion. Indicator of mineral metabolic profile and acid-base balance; potassium depletion decreases intracellular pH and increases H+ secretion into the tubular lumen. Excretion of excess potassium; involved in renal acid-base balance and systemic electrolyte regulation.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: K citrate supplementation in postmenopausal women. Pre-treatment metabolic features in osteopenic women, indicating low-grade metabolic acidosis. K citrate supplementation aimed to normalize these defects.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Increased potassium excretion indicates a positive effect of K citrate supplementation on mineral metabolism, correlating directly with increased urinary pH (R=0.33, p=0.02) and citrate excretion (R=0.47, p=0.002). Consistent with low-grade metabolic acidosis which promotes bone loss and favors precipitation of calcium salts. Suggested subjects conserve this alkali element to maintain normal serum levels. Indicator of renal potassium handling and systemic acid-base balance, particularly relevant to K citrate intake.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Levels were largely variable. PINP levels increased in patients with low pH and low citrate excretion treated with K citrate, while they decreased in the placebo group; however, high variability of the data did not allow pointing out significant differences. PINP correlated significantly with 24h citrate excretion in the entire population (R=0.24, p=0.003) and with pH values in the subgroup with low pH in fasting-morning urine (R=0.31; p=0.003). An increase was suggested in the last three-month period, indicating an anabolic effect. An increase in PINP levels after K citrate supplementation has also been described by Jehle et al. [44].

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Fragment cleaved from procollagen during the synthesis of type I collagen, serving as a marker of bone formation. Reflects the production of type I collagen by osteoblasts (OBs) and is found in highest concentration during the proliferative phase of bone remodeling.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: K citrate supplementation in postmenopausal women, particularly those with baseline low urinary pH or citrate excretion. K citrate supplementation in osteopenic women (anabolic effect observed in the last three months).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: While overall changes were variable, the observed increase in specific K citrate-treated subgroups with baseline defects suggests a potential positive impact on bone formation, although not statistically significant due to data variability. Correlation with urinary parameters indicates a link to mineral metabolism. Reflects bone remodeling unit (BRU) activity and correlates with bone loss. Considered a useful tool for assessing response to anti-osteoporotic drugs and recommended by international committees as a reference marker for bone formation. Increases rapidly after anabolic agents like teriparatide.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Tended to increase after treatment with K citrate. No notable or significant results were found (data not shown). A variable increase was observed, which was difficult to interpret. The increase could reflect a growing osteoclast number. TRACP5b has generally not been investigated in clinical trials regarding K citrate in osteopenic women.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Enzyme primarily produced by osteoclasts, serving as a specific marker for osteoclast number and bone resorption activity.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: K citrate supplementation in postmenopausal women. K citrate supplementation in osteopenic women (observed increase hypothesized to reflect growing osteoclast number to maintain bone homeostasis).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: An unexpected tendency to increase, though not significant, suggests K citrate did not improve (and possibly slightly worsened) this specific marker of osteoclast activity, implying no beneficial effect on this aspect of bone resorption. Reflects bone remodeling unit (BRU) activity and correlates with bone loss. Considered a useful tool for assessing response to anti-osteoporotic drugs, but clinical usefulness data are not always consistent.
